notes.b: A will is a legal document, governed by the Succession Act 1965, in which a person (the testator) sets out how their property and money, known as the estate, are to be shared after their death. Making one means your wishes are followed instead of leaving the decision to the law.
points: Without a will (called intestacy), the estate passes under fixed rules in the Succession Act that set the shares, and these may not match the person's wishes.

Under those fixed rules a spouse with no children takes the whole estate, and a spouse with children takes two thirds while the children share one third. Other relatives inherit only if there is no spouse or children, and the State inherits only if there are no relatives.
A will allows the testator to choose who receives each item of property and in what proportions, so the property passes to the people they want.
A will names an executor (the person who carries out the will), who collects the estate, pays the debts and distributes the property as the will directs.
A will can protect a spouse and dependants, and it can state the testator's funeral or burial wishes.
A clearly drawn will reduces the likelihood of disputes among family members over the estate, and it gives the testator peace of mind.
Parents can use a will to appoint a guardian for young children and to make suitable provision for them.

Divorced parents who make a will can ensure that property passes to their children as they intend, can choose an executor, and can change the will later if circumstances alter, such as remarriage or new children.
Careful planning of a will, with a solicitor's advice, may reduce the inheritance tax burden on those who inherit.
notes.tip: Examiners ask you to state why a will is important and to outline the procedure, and they expect the two halves in balance (about seven points in all). For divorced parents, say the property passes as intended, the will can be changed after remarriage or new children, and an executor is chosen. Do not write that the State gets a large part of the estate when there is no will: it inherits only if there are no relatives.

notes.h: Legal requirements for a valid will
notes.b: The law sets simple rules so that a will really reflects what the testator wanted. If a rule is broken, the will may not be valid.
points: The testator must be 18 or over (or be or have been married), because the law treats them as old enough to make this decision.
The testator must be of sound mind, meaning able to understand what a will is and what property they own, so that the will reflects their real wishes.
The will must be in writing, and it must be signed by the testator or by someone signing for them in their presence and at their direction.
The signature must be made, or acknowledged, in the presence of two witnesses who are both present at the same time.
The witnesses then sign the will in the presence of the testator.

A witness, or the witness's spouse, who is also a beneficiary (someone who is given a gift in the will) loses the gift made to them under the will, which is why witnesses should be people with nothing to gain. The executor, however, can be a beneficiary.
Good practice is to date the will, store it safely (for example with the solicitor or in a bank) and tell the executor where it is kept, so that it can be found after the death.
notes.tip: When asked for three features of a valid will, choose from: 18 or over, sound mind, in writing, signed before two witnesses, an executor chosen. Dating is good practice that marking schemes credit, but the Act does not make it a legal requirement.

notes.b: Making a will is a matter of working out what you own and who should get it, then putting that in a form the law accepts. It follows six steps.
points: Step 1: list all assets, such as property, savings, investments, policies and personal possessions, with their value and location, and any debts or liabilities, so you know what the estate contains.
Step 2: decide who the beneficiaries are, starting with the nearest relatives, and record their full names and addresses and the item or share each is to receive.
Step 3: appoint an executor, a trusted person who is willing to act and who will collect the estate, pay the debts and carry out the terms.

Step 4: decide how the estate is divided, including any specific gifts, provision for children and dependants, any guardian, and any funeral or burial arrangements the testator wishes to make. Check this against the legal restrictions in the Succession Act.
Step 5: have the will drawn up. A person may write their own will, but a solicitor is advised so that it is clear and valid.
Step 6: sign the will before two witnesses, store the signed will safely, and tell the executor where it is kept.
After the death, the executor applies for a grant of probate, which confirms the will and gives the executor legal authority to deal with the estate.
notes.tip: For a procedure question, give about four steps with detail, in order. A will does not take effect until the testator dies.

notes.b: A will can be changed at any time while the testator is of sound mind, because it takes effect only on death. The law allows several ways of changing or cancelling it.
points: A change to an existing will can be made by a codicil, a short document added to the will, which must be signed and witnessed in the same way as the original will.
A new will that expressly revokes (cancels) an earlier will replaces it entirely.
A will can also be revoked by destroying it with that intention.
A will is revoked by the testator's marriage (or civil partnership), unless the will was made in contemplation of that marriage. This is why remarrying parents must make a new will.
notes.tip: A codicil is not a new will: it only amends the existing one. Divorce or judicial separation does not itself revoke a will, so do not claim that it does.

notes.h: Limits on what a will can do
notes.b: A testator is free to choose who inherits, but not completely free. The law protects a surviving spouse, and it gives the executor a formal step to carry out.
points: A surviving spouse (or civil partner) has a legal right to a share of the estate that the will cannot remove: one-half where there are no children, and one-third where there are children.

Children cannot be left out without thought: a child may ask the court for fair provision if the parent failed in their moral duty to them. Where there is a will, children have no automatic fixed share.
Executors apply for a grant of probate, which confirms the will and gives the executor authority to deal with the estate.
notes.tip: Learn the shares correctly. In a will, the spouse's legal right is one half with no children and one third with children. Without a will, a spouse with children takes two thirds and the children share one third. Do not say children are entitled to two thirds.

keyTerms.definition: A person who makes a will, setting out how their estate is to be distributed after death.
All the property, money and possessions a person owns at death, which is distributed under their will or under the rules of intestacy.
The person named in a will to collect the estate, pay debts and distribute property as the will directs.
A person or organisation who receives property or money under a will.
A document that amends an existing will, signed and witnessed in the same way as the will itself.
The mental capacity to understand what a will is and the effect it will have on the property it covers.
A share of the estate that a surviving spouse is entitled to receive regardless of what the will says.

questions.prompt: Explain why it is particularly important for divorced parents to make a will.
questions.model: A will ensures that property and personal items pass to the children and other beneficiaries as the parent intends, rather than under fixed statutory rules. It allows the parent to appoint an executor to collect the estate and carry out the wishes. The will can be changed later if circumstances alter, and a clear will reduces the risk of disputes among family members.

questions.prompt: Outline the importance of making a will and the procedure involved in making a valid will.
questions.model: A will allows a person to decide who receives their estate and in what shares, and to appoint an executor to carry out their wishes. Without a will, fixed statutory rules set the shares and may not match the person's intentions. The testator must be over 18 and of sound mind. The procedure begins by listing the assets and debts and recording the beneficiaries. An executor is appointed and the estate is allocated, including any specific gifts. The will is then drawn up, often by a solicitor, signed in writing and witnessed by two witnesses present together, who sign in the testator's presence. The signed will should be stored safely and the executor told where it is kept. A later marriage revokes the will unless it was made in contemplation of that marriage, so the will should be reviewed.
